history.heading: Mother colony of the Caribbean
paragraphs: Saint Kitts and Nevis, two volcanic islands in the Leeward Islands, were inhabited by Kalinago people, who called St Kitts Liamuiga, "fertile land". English settlers established a colony on St Kitts in 1623, the first English colony in the Caribbean, and the French settled the other end of the island. In 1626 English and French settlers massacred the Kalinago at Bloody Point.

Sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans made the islands very profitable. Brimstone Hill Fortress, a large British fortress, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Alexander Hamilton, a founding father of the United States, was born on Nevis in 1755.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Britain gained full control in 1783. Slavery was abolished in 1834. The islands were united with Anguilla in a colony, from which Anguilla separated in 1967–1980. Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent on 19 September 1983. Nevis voted on secession in 1998, narrowly failing to reach the required two-thirds majority.

culture.heading: Island culture
paragraphs: English is official, and a local Creole is widely spoken. Most people are Christian. Carnival around Christmas and New Year, and the St Kitts Music Festival, are highlights. Stewed saltfish with dumplings and breadfruit is the national dish.

politics.heading: Federal parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Saint Kitts and Nevis is a federal parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch represented by a governor-general. It is the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere. Nevis has its own assembly and premier and the constitutional right to secede.

economy.heading: Tourism and citizenship
paragraphs: Sugar production ended in 2005. The economy now relies on tourism, offshore finance, and the world's oldest citizenship-by-investment programme, started in 1984, which provides a large share of government revenue. The currency is the Eastern Caribbean dollar.
